chunks: "Charge pumps are used when I need a voltage outside the supply range at fairly low current and I don't want an inductor.
The big ones: a negative rail from a positive supply, for op-amp or ADC front ends or LCD contrast.
RS-232 transceivers, which make about plus and minus 10 volts from 5 volts or 3. 3 volts. White-LED backlight and flash drivers, where a 1x, 1.
5x or 2x pump keeps the LEDs lit as a Li-ion cell falls from 4. 2 to 3 volts. Gate-drive supplies, to turn on a high-side N-FET or a load switch above the rail.
And on-chip high voltages: flash and EEPROM programming, DRAM word-line boost, and bias for RF switches or MEMS.
I'd choose a pump over an inductive boost for small loads, up to a couple of hundred milliamps: it takes less board area, there's no inductor to pick, and EMI is easier.
I'd go inductive when I need amps, a continuously adjustable output, or high efficiency across a wide input range, because a pump's efficiency is capped by V out over (nV in) .
And I'd note that a PLL's charge pump is something else entirely."
